name: Ancient sites and mysteries
question: Which sites of ancient history are here (lost civilisations, mysterious temples and megaliths, underground cities, submerged ruins and sunken cities), and how can a visitor reach them lawfully: opening, tickets, permits, guides, closures, photography, diving, and the heritage laws and penalties that protect them?
sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (whc.unesco.org) and the UNESCO 2001 Convention states parties list
national heritage or antiquities ministries and their site pages
park and site authorities (for example Heritage Malta, English Heritage, Angkor Enterprise, Parco Archeologico dei Campi Flegrei)
fields: sites[]: name, place (place id), kind, era, what, access {opening, tickets, permits, guide, closures, photography}, protection {law, penalties}, underwater {diving, guide_or_permit, law, unesco_2001, penalties} (underwater sites only), lore {text, source (url or null), label}, sources[], checked
rules: Facts (name, era, what it is, access, protection, diving) come only from official sources: UNESCO, national heritage or antiquities authorities, park or site authorities and official tourism boards.

The lore field holds popular legends and theories (ancient aliens, lost civilisations, portals or stargates, subterranean networks, Atlantis) as claims, never facts. Start with 'Popular theories claim' or 'Local legend says'. If an official page mentions the legend, cite it in lore.source; otherwise set lore.label to 'popular lore, not an official source' and keep it brief and neutral.
Unchecked access details say 'not yet checked'. Never infer opening hours, prices or diving permission.

Underwater sites: record whether recreational diving is allowed, any licensed guide or permit, the national underwater cultural heritage law and whether the country is a party to the UNESCO 2001 Convention.

Stack layout: the country record holds national heritage law and sites; region or site records hold access rules that differ there. Note the Smartraveller advice level where it is Reconsider or Do not travel.

Themes link popular legends to real visitable places. A theme line is lore, never fact; tag sites with theme ids. A documented science fact attached to a theme (for example geomagnetic reversals from USGS) stays in its own fact field with its source.
Ancient temples are included only when ancient or legendary with notable mystery or lore attached (for example Kailasa, Borobudur, Konark). Modern working temples are not added for completeness.

themes.name: Shambhala
themes.lore: Lore: a hidden Buddhist kingdom of the Kalachakra tradition, said by popular theories to lie somewhere in the Himalaya or Central Asia.

themes.name: Shangri-La
themes.lore: Lore: a fictional hidden valley from James Hilton's 1933 novel Lost Horizon, now claimed by several Himalayan places.

themes.name: Norse myth
themes.lore: Lore: gods, giants and the world tree of the Norse sagas, linked in popular tradition to royal mounds and temple sites in Scandinavia.

themes.name: Greek myth
themes.lore: Lore: oracles, labyrinths and gods of Greek myth, such as the Delphic oracle and the Minotaur's labyrinth at Knossos.

themes.name: Sumerian
themes.lore: Lore: popular theories claim Sumerian texts describe visitors from another planet (the Anunnaki); scholars read them as myth.

themes.name: Mt Shasta
themes.lore: Lore: popular theories claim a hidden city (Telos) of survivors from Lemuria lies inside the mountain.

themes.name: Mt Hayes (Alaska)
themes.lore: Lore: online popular theories claim a hidden structure or pyramid in the Alaska Range near Mt Hayes.

themes.name: Naga
themes.lore: Lore: serpent deities of Hindu and Buddhist tradition, said in Mekong legend to live in the river and guard temples.

themes.name: Hopi ant people
themes.lore: Lore: popular theories retell a Hopi account of 'ant people' who sheltered the Hopi underground, and link it to visitors from the sky. These are outside claims, not Hopi teaching as recorded by the Tribe.

themes.name: Atlantis
themes.lore: Lore: Plato's island that sank in a day and a night; popular theories place it at many real sites.

themes.name: Lemuria
themes.lore: Lore: a lost continent first proposed in 19th-century science and now a popular legend of a sunken Pacific or Indian Ocean civilisation.

themes.name: Mu
themes.lore: Lore: a lost Pacific continent popularised in the 1920s, linked by popular theories to Yonaguni and Nan Madol.

themes.name: Antarctica lost civilisation and pole shift
themes.lore: Lore: popular theories claim Antarctica held a lost civilisation before a sudden physical pole shift moved the crust. Kept apart from the documented fact of geomagnetic reversals (see fact).

fact.text: Earth's magnetic field has reversed polarity many times, recorded in lavas and sediments; reversals have no set period (from about 10,000 to over 50 million years apart), take hundreds to thousands of years, and the last was about 780,000 years ago. This is a magnetic reversal, not a physical shift of the crust or poles.

themes.name: Hidden-realm caves
themes.lore: Lore: caves said in legend to lead to hidden or underworld realms, such as Xibalba, Patala, Hades, Agartha, Telos, the hollow earth and the beyul hidden valleys.
